check: verify goal item 3's certificate against the log it transcribes, and verify its freshness claim against git
why: The certificate says it is transcribed verbatim because the run directory was deleted for disk space, so the only surviving source is a 17.68 GB log. Transcription is exactly the step where a claim can drift from its evidence, and it is checkable.

theTranscriptionIsExact.method: Streamed the log as UTF-16LE - the encoding its first bytes FF FE confirm - and compared each of the three transcribed lines character for character
theTranscriptionIsExact.line743968: REAL_WALL_TRAVERSAL_PASS owners=505 voxels=28046 feet=2537 reopen=false production=OFF - identical
theTranscriptionIsExact.significance: The three lines sit at the very end of the log, which is where a successful build ends, and each matches exactly rather than approximately.

theFreshnessClaimHolds.claim: The traversal ran 4.2 hours after src/main last changed and no src/main change followed it
theFreshnessClaimHolds.checkedWithGit: git log 6e67cc2..HEAD -- src/main returns zero commits, and 6e67cc2 is the last commit touching src/main at all. Cross-checked from 50a1245 as well: also zero.
theFreshnessClaimHolds.soTheRunExercisedCurrentSource: The certificate's own reason for recording this was that it had not named a commit, so the timeline had to be reconstructed from the run directory name, log timestamps and git. Recording it means the next reader does not repeat that work - and it still holds.

whatCouldNotBeChecked: The run directory wallpass20261006212921 is gone, so the runStarted time derived from its name cannot be re-derived. The finish side is corroborated by the log's final timestamp 03:13:11 against the certificate's runFinished of 2026-10-07 03:13:13.
conclusion: Goal item 3's certificate is accurate where it can be checked, and the one claim that could have drifted - the verbatim transcription - is exact.
